package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x, y := 3, 8
	p := &x
	q := p
	p = &y
	fmt.Println(*q)
	fmt.Println(*p)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x, y := 1, 9
	p := &x
	pp := &p
	*pp = &y
	fmt.Println(*p)
}
Which methods are in the method set of *T?
options: Methods with receiver T and with *T
Only methods with receiver *T
Only methods with receiver T
None: only T has methods

questions.text: Which methods are in the method set of T?
options: Methods of T and *T
Only methods with receiver T
Only methods with receiver *T
None

questions.text: Why does t.bump() compile when bump has receiver *T and t is an addressable T?
options: T is automatically copied to the heap
The value receiver is called instead
The compiler calls (&t).bump()
It works only inside the same package

questions.text: Does a pointer-receiver method run when the receiver is nil?
options: No. A nil receiver is a compile error
No. Any such call panics at once
Yes, but only for exported methods
Yes. It panics only if the method touches fields

questions.text: Why is var i any = (*T)(nil) not equal to nil?
options: The interface holds type *T; it is a typed nil, not an empty interface
nil cannot be stored in any
(*T)(nil) is not actually nil
any compares by field values

questions.text: Why does for _, v := range s on []T not change s’s elements?
options: range forbids writes to structs
v is a copy of the element
The whole slice is copied for range
v has type *T

questions.text: Why does for _, v := range s on []*T mutate the objects?
options: range does not copy pointers
v is an index, not a copy
The pointer is copied; the object behind it is the same
It works only for nil pointers

questions.text: How do you update a struct value in a map if you cannot take &m[k]?
options: The only way is unsafe
Call a pointer-receiver method on m[k]
It is impossible: map values are immutable
Read it, change the copy, write it back

questions.text: How does *[]T differ from []*T?
options: *[]T is a pointer to a slice header; []*T is a slice of pointers to elements
They are two names for the same type
*[]T cannot be passed to append
[]*T stores elements inside the pointer itself

questions.text: What happens to a local if a function returns &x?
options: A dangling pointer
The compiler forbids return &x
x is copied; the pointer refers to the caller’s stack
The compiler moves it to the heap; the pointer stays valid

questions.text: Why does v.bump() in a range over []T not change the slice when bump is a pointer receiver?
options: &v is the address of the copy, not the slice cell
A pointer receiver cannot be called from range
bump copies the slice
v in range has type T and is not addressable

questions.text: Can you assign *T to an interface whose method set is only T’s methods?
options: No: the interface needs exactly T
Yes: *T’s method set includes T’s methods
Yes, but only if T is not addressable
No, until there are methods with receiver *T

questions.text: Can you assign a T to an interface that needs a method with receiver *T?
options: Yes, the compiler always takes &T
Yes if T is comparable
No: T’s method set does not include that method
Only if T is a zero value

questions.text: What does p = q do to two *T values if you do not touch *p?
options: The old object’s contents are copied into the new one
Both pointers become nil
It is a compile error
p now points where q points; the old object is unchanged

questions.text: Why does map[string]*T allow m["a"].n = 9?
options: The map yields a copy of the pointer; the field changes in the shared object
A map element is addressable when it is a pointer
The compiler takes &m["a"] for you
It works only for string keys

questions.text: Is p + 1 allowed for *T in safe Go?
options: Yes, as in C
No. Address offset is only through unsafe
Yes if T is an array
Yes for *byte

questions.answer: To replace the caller’s slice header.

questions.text: What is copied when you copy a struct with an *Inner field?
questions.answer: The Inner address, not Inner itself.

questions.answer: It has no memory slot whose address can be taken.
